searches.note: Thirty one searches of a share of forty five, fourteen left unspent. One was shared across the group: the decree of 2018 that made Apalta and Los Lingues areas of the Colchagua Valley. Thirteen were restricted to a house's own domain (Montes four times, once with its importer beside it, Clos Apalta twice, Casa Silva four times, Viu Manent twice, González Byass once); the rest blocked the house's domain, where the author had leant on it, so that each second source would be independent. One search for the Spanish Alpha M sheet returned nothing of use and is counted. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a claim was stated more strongly than any source seen (twenty years of ageing, advice laid at a house's door, every grape destemmed by hand in every vintage) it was said with less; where a detail stood in no source read or cited (concrete eggs at Neyen, critics' drinking windows, Le Petit Clos as Carmenère led) it was cut.

A making detail the author read on a house's own sheet and that no sheet seen here contradicted stands on that one primary source and is listed as open (the Montes harvest into small boxes, the punching down by hand at Clos Apalta, Neyen's native yeasts and tanks of 5,000 litres).
Wine Spectator's Wine of the Year is cut as a rating, as the Friuli and Montalcino refuters ruled for a guide's or a magazine's wine of the year.

Writers' own sites and blogs met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, Talk-a-Vino, Wine Peeps, a Wordpress photographer's blog, an encyclopaedia written by a language model) are cited neither in the fragment nor here; a profile whose title names a living winemaker is described, never cited.
The serving temperatures follow the Codex's service reference, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius for the five full reds; no air is promised to soften tannin.

The edits were made in place by exact replacement of the author's strings, keeping the author's layout (the file is written as the author wrote it, one space of indent), and linted sound with five records refuted.

tested: The first harvest of 1987 and the founding of 1988 as Discover Wines: the house's timeline (primary), and the importer Kobrand for four partners in 1988 and the name; Liberty Wines and others date the venture to 1987. Sound, the house's own dates.
Viña Montes as a later name: the timeline says founded initially as Discover Wines and gives no year for the change; soon was nowhere. Changed to later.
The Apalta estate of 1995: the house's timeline; Wine Spectator gives 1991 for the first land bought in Apalta and Decanter's Wine Legend 1989. Kept as the timeline's, which the story names; open.

Alpha M from the 1996 vintage: the house, Kobrand and several merchants. Sound. The house's timeline calls it Chile's first iconic wine, with Folly the first iconic Syrah in 2000 and Purple Angel the first iconic Carmenère in 2003; the judging word is taken out and the dates put in.

The blend, about four fifths Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot (80, 10, 5, 5 on the sheets), on the granite of the Finca de Apalta: the house's sheets through a distributor's copy, Kobrand for the upper, low yielding blocks on thin soils. Sound.

The making: five days of cold soak at about 9 degrees, ten days of fermentation at 28 with selected yeasts and eighteen months in French oak, about 80 per cent new on the sheet for 2017 and 70 on a review of 2020, all new in the early vintages by Decanter and the house's shop. Sound. Small boxes, the cool of the day and the fall by gravity into stainless steel were in no sheet seen here; the winery's gravity design is confirmed by Meininger's and WineLand; open.

The winery of December 2004 on feng shui principles: the house's cellar page, WineLand, Meininger's and Sommelier India. Sound. The Gregorian chant the author left out is told by WineLand and others, with hours that disagree; it stays out.

The ageing of twenty years and more by the house's sheets: no Alpha M sheet seen gives a figure; the house's sheets for its Alpha Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah give ten years and more. Changed. The decanting of at least an hour as the house advises: the Alpha sheets advise about thirty minutes. Changed.

Apalta as an area of the decree since 2018: the shared search. Sound. Cards and questions: one right answer each, four options of one kind, the explanations teach; Discover Wines as the key stands on the house and Kobrand. Rules: the founding winemaker and partners are never named; no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

open: The year the Apalta estate was bought: 1995 in the house's timeline, which the story follows and names as its source, 1991 in Wine Spectator and 1989 in Decanter's Wine Legend.

The picking into small boxes, the sorting by bunch and the fall by gravity into stainless steel rest on the author's reading of the house's sheet for 2020; the sheets for 2017 and 2021 seen here confirm the five days of cold soak at about 9 degrees, the ten days of fermentation and the eighteen months in French oak, and the importer the selection by hand and by berry.

tested: Louis-Alexandre Marnier Lapostolle, 4 March 1857 to 29 January 1930, and Grand Marnier of 1880, cognac with bitter orange: Wikipedia's pages on the man and the liqueur, Difford's Guide and Wein-Plus. Sound.
The founding of 1994 by a couple of the family, with the old Apalta vineyard: BK Wine Magazine, Berry Bros. and Rudd, Wine Spectator's interview, the library. Sound; the couple are not named.
The first Clos Apalta of 1997: BK Wine Magazine, which adds that none was made in 1998, and the house's pages. Sound.

The old vines: pre phylloxera Carmenère and Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1920 and never grafted on the house's sheets, the 1910s on a later sheet, 1915 to 1940 on the sheet for 2016, a French massal selection, colluvial granite with layers of clay. The record's early twentieth century and its sites stand.

The making: all grapes destemmed by hand on the sheets for 2014 and 2015, but only 18 per cent of the 2003 on the house's page for that vintage; 77 to 100 per cent fermented in vats of 75 hectolitres; skin contact up to five weeks (2012); malolactic in barrel; 24 to 28 months in new barriques (2012 to 2015); unfiltered (2003, 2013, 2014). Hand destemming changed to the later vintages; the rest sound.

The gravity winery: confirmed by Lay and Wheeler, Winebow and the house; its year, 2004 on one trade page, stays out. Biodynamic and organic farming of the vineyards: the library and one importer's page. Sound.

Wine Spectator's Wine of the Year for the 2005, named in 2008: true by the house and several merchants, but a magazine's ranking is a rating, refused anywhere by the brief and by the Friuli and Montalcino rulings. Cut, with the claim of the first Chilean wine so named.
Le Petit Clos: on the house's sheets from 2014 as a Bordeaux blend from Apalta; no sheet read said Carmenère led. Changed. Cuvée Alexandre: the library. Sound.

Cards and questions: one right answer each; the wine question's options are four grapes and the key is not the longest; the story question's explanation is rewritten to teach without the rating. Rules: the family's living members and the consultant are never named; the trap's Don Melchor is a wine, not a person; no price, no score once the ranking is out, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

tested: The ancestor: the house has him reach Chile in 1887 at 22 from near Saint-Émilion to work as an oenologist and viticulturist, and buy Angostura with his family in 1910 (1912 for the winery and the plantings on other pages); TasteAtlas and a winemaker's profile give 1887; Frommer's and a tour guide give 1892 for his first vines. The story's late nineteenth century and early twentieth stand; trained in Bordeaux is changed to from near Saint-Émilion.

The restoration from the late 1970s (1977 or 1978 on the house's pages) and the founding of Viña Casa Silva in 1997 on the proposal of the eldest son of the fifth generation, ending the bulk sales: the house, Wine Peeps (a blog, not cited) and the merchants. Sound; April is the house's own date.

The soil study of 2005 with the University of Talca, three years of microvinification by plot: the house's research page, The Drinks Business of 2009 and a winemaker's profile (not cited, its title naming him). Sound; the claim of the first such study in Chile is told as the house's.

The selection: a selection of the best plants from each block, in the house's words. Changed to plants selected in each block. The first vintage of 2005 is one merchant's; left out, as the author did.

The making on the sheet for 2021: chilled to 5 degrees, ten days of cold soak at 6, sixteen days of fermentation in French oak barrels of 500 litres and foudres of 1,000 at 25 to 28, twenty days of maceration after, malolactic in barrels of 500 litres, fifteen months in French oak. Sound.
The origin: the sheet for 2021 gives D.O. Valle de Colchagua, while S7 carries D.O. Los Lingues. The appellation is changed to Colchagua Valley and the label line says so.
The site: the house places Los Lingues in the Andean foothills; no source read gave north east; the decree puts the area in the commune of San Fernando. Changed to the eastern edge.
The ageing: about fifteen years on the house's page, not fifteen to twenty. Changed. The house serves it at 15 to 16 degrees; the record keeps the Codex's 16 to 18; open.

S7 as Carmenère from a single block (the best cuartel of the variety at Los Lingues, by the house) and 1912 Vines Sauvignon Gris named for the year of the Angostura plantings: the house's pages. Sound. Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind (1892 is the date some give for the ancestor's vines), explanations that teach. Rules: the founder of 1997, his father, the winemaker and the professor are never named; no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

The Hacienda San Carlos de Cunaco bought by one of the sons in 1966: the house, Wikipedia, Cellar Tours. Sound.

The first Chilean wine of Malbec alone under the grape's name in 1993: the house's milestones and its notice of thirty years, and a vineyards list; told as the house's account, Wikipedia no longer named beside it. Changed in wording.
Viu 1 from the 1999 vintage, as a tribute to the son who bought the estate: the house, the importer Grape and Cellier; one producer profile gives 2001, read as the year of release. Sound.

The editions: the house's sheets number the 2019 the eighteenth, the 2020 the nineteenth and the 2021 the twentieth; one merchant says twenty first. The house's count stands, and each vintage since is changed to each vintage made, as some years were not made. The numbered bottles: the house's shop. Sound.
Block 4 of San Carlos, planted more than a century ago, on alluvial sandy clay with very good drainage: the house's sheets for 2019, 2020 and 2021. Sound.

The blend and the making on the sheet for 2021: 83 per cent Malbec and 17 Cabernet Sauvignon (85, 14 and 1 Petit Verdot in 2020; 86, 12 and 2 in 2019), twenty one days on the skins in all, fifteen months in untoasted French foudres (55 per cent) and barriques (45), unfiltered. Sound.

The ageing: ten to twelve years on the icon page, up to ten on the sheet for 2021. Changed to about a decade by the house's own pages. Secreto's fifteen per cent of secret grapes: the house's sheets for 2015 and 2022. Sound.

Cards and questions: one right answer each; the story question's distractors are the house's own years. Rules: the founder, his sons and the family's present head are never named; no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

tested: The vines: González Byass gives Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère planted in 1890 and 1936, never grafted, and the oldest winery in Apalta with walls of 1890; Wine Industry Advisor has the walls in 1890 and the Cabernet planted the year before; Decanter gives 1889 in one piece and 1890 for both in another. Carmenère of 1936 is consistent. The Cabernet changed to about 1890 throughout; the oldest in the valley changed to the oldest in Apalta.
The owners: the Rojas family bought the property in 1970 by Decanter, 1973 by Wine Industry Advisor and a tour guide, and sold its fruit to others for decades. Added as the early 1970s.

Neyen created in 2002 (Wine Industry Advisor; the new winery of 2002 in Decanter's merger report) with the first vintage in 2003 (Decanter's Colchagua feature; twenty years of winemaking marked in July 2023). Added in place of the early 2000s.

González Byass's majority of Veramonte in June 2016, with Neyen, Primus and the Apalta estate, the Rojas family keeping a minority: González Byass's own news, Diario Financiero, Decanter and Shanken. Sound. Torres at Curicó in 1979: the Codex's own records. Sound.

The blend: about half and half in recent vintages (55 Cabernet Sauvignon and 45 Carmenère in 2019 by one listing, 55 Carmenère in 2013 by another), 50, 33 and 17 Petit Verdot in 2006. a little Petit Verdot changed to Petit Verdot as well.

The making: picked at first light and double sorted (González Byass's sheet for 2015), fourteen months in French barrels and six in foudres of 3,000 litres (merchants for 2017 and 2018). Sound. Native yeasts and tanks of 5,000 litres stand on the author's reading of the Veramonte sheet; open. Concrete eggs in later vintages were in no source; cut.
The ageing: the critics' windows and the importer's figure stood in no cited source; merchants give ten years and more. Changed.
The name: González Byass glosses Neyen as the spirit of Apalta, the name known locally; the Mapuche origin stays out, as the author left it. Sound.

Cards and questions: one right answer each; the wine question's key no longer gives a year more exact than the sources. Rules: the Rojas family is a family, its head and the seller and consultant are never named; no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

shared.search: The decree of 2018 that made Apalta and Los Lingues areas of the Colchagua Valley
shared.finding: Four new areas were gazetted in 2018 (Lo Abarca, Licantén, Apalta and Los Lingues) under Decreto 112 of that year, amending Decreto 464 of 1994; the amended decree defines Apalta by the rural locality of that name in the commune of Santa Cruz and Los Lingues by the rural locality in the commune of San Fernando. The since 2018 of the Montes, Lapostolle and Casa Silva records stands. A court case over the creation of Los Lingues, against a trademark of 2013, was met; its outcome was not found.

swaps.proposed: The author proposed no swap and kept the plan's five houses and their wines.
swaps.why: Nothing in this check rules a pick out: Montes Alpha M, Clos Apalta, Casa Silva's Microterroir (the house's own highest Carmenère), Viu 1 and Neyen Espíritu de Apalta are each the wine its house leads with, and the label of each was seen in the searches; nothing is to be changed in plan.json.

picks: All five picks stand. For the chunk's read-together agent: the plan's why for casa-silva says the family has been in Colchagua since 1892, where the house dates its ancestor's arrival in Chile to 1887 and its Angostura estate to 1910, and independent pages give 1887 or 1892; the late nineteenth century would hold. The why for neyen says Carmenère and Cabernet were planted in 1890; the house dates the Cabernet to about 1890 (1889 in one of its accounts) and the Carmenère to 1936.
Casa Silva's blend Altura is the house's other high wine; Microterroir is kept, as the house calls it its highest expression of Carmenère and the pick teaches the grape.
